title: Mobile Game A: acquisition analytics
decision: A mobile-game team must decide whether to shift acquisition spend across its eight campaigns (A–H) after one month of cost and player-activity data.
provenance: Assessment data · anonymized · real, not synthetic

sections.heading: What this page shows
paragraphs: The notebook compares eight acquisition campaigns on cost per day-7 payer, funnel rates, and revenue per registered player, then sizes a follow-up experiment. Every number below is computed from the four files in the repository — drag the controls and the answers change with them.
The data is real: records from a mobile-game hiring assessment, employer and game anonymized. This is a portfolio demonstration, not a client outcome.

sections.heading: Which campaigns clear the $50 screen?
paragraphs: CPP divides a campaign's May cost by its day-7 payers — a payer is a registered user with at least one payment within 168 hours of registration. The screen labels CPP ≤ $50 as meets target and CPP > $50 as above target.

Drag the threshold. Campaign membership, the funnel below, and the caption recompute together. At the default $50, three campaigns meet the screen: B at $40.00, E at $43.70, G at $44.80. The pooled gap in tutorial completion (53.85% vs 47.17%) describes the groups; it does not show that cheap campaigns produce better players.

sections.heading: Does the ranking hold across observation windows?
paragraphs: ARPU divides in-window payment revenue by registered users in the campaign, with non-payers kept at zero. Each line follows one campaign across the observation windows: values rise, lines cross, and longer windows silently include registrants who never had a full follow-up period — which understates their ARPU.

There is also a definitional trap in the source notebook: two window rules disagree for the same metric (see the note under the chart). The rule, not the data, explains the difference — so any ARPU number in a report is meaningless without its window contract.

sections.heading: Campaign E vs H: what the test actually saw
paragraphs: Campaign E's strict 168-hour ARPU is $0.68; campaign H's is $0.29. A Mann–Whitney U test on user-level payment totals reports p ≈ 0.0007. Both distributions are skewed with a large mass of zeros — the curve below shows the full distribution at once: at any $x, the share of users whose 7-day total reaches it.

Two caveats travel with that p-value: no effect size or confidence interval is reported, and the E/H pair was selected after inspecting the data. Treat it as a lead worth a clean experiment, not as a finding.

sections.heading: Exploratory cohort revenue curve
paragraphs: The notebook's last figure follows 5,421 users who registered between May 10 and May 20 (the query's date filter) and completed the tutorial within 168 hours, then plots their cumulative payment revenue over the first 100 whole-day steps after registration. The curve ends near $467.

It renders the notebook's SQL exactly as written, defects and all: daily revenue is not aggregated before the cumulative sum, and elapsed days are truncated to whole days. Read it as a map of the cohort method and its traps — not as an LTV estimate.

sections.heading: Design the next test
paragraphs: Campaign E's baseline day-3 payer conversion is 4.17%. The notebook sizes a follow-up experiment for a 20% relative improvement: about 7,764 users per arm for a one-sided test at α = 0.05 with 80% power — roughly 15.5 days at 1,000 daily registrations.

Move the sliders to price other targets. The formula behind the readout is the one the notebook uses; eligibility rules, exposure logging, guardrails and a stopping rule still have to be defined before this becomes a real test.

sections.heading: What this cannot show
items: Campaign comparisons are observational. Nothing here shows that a campaign caused higher-value players.
The day-7 payer filter accepts payments logged before registration, and cost dates are not aligned to registration cohorts.
The two ARPU window rules disagree ($0.75 vs $0.68 for campaign E at 7 days), and longer windows include registrants without full follow-up.
The cohort SQL in the notebook does not aggregate daily revenue before its cumulative sum and truncates elapsed days — its curve is not a validated LTV estimate.
The E/H test reports a p-value without an effect size or confidence interval, and the pair was selected on the same data.
The 6,686 registrations without a campaign value drop out of all campaign-level denominators.
Publication permission for the assessment CSVs is not confirmed.

sections.heading: Run it yourself
paragraphs: The notebook regenerates every number and figure on this page in one clean run; the four CSVs ship with the repository. In Google Colab, clone the repository in the first cell (!git clone https://github.com/biziman/data-analyst-case-studies followed by %cd data-analyst-case-studies), then run all.
Metric definitions, tested package versions and the full list of open review items live in the case README.
